7.59400,47.56700.name: Novartis — gene therapy
7.59400,47.56700.desc: Sells Zolgensma, a one-dose gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy, at over two million dollars. Novartis is the case that makes the pricing argument concrete: a company of this size, with this much manufacturing capacity, still prices a single-dose cure at the outer edge of what health systems will pay — which is a decision about what the market will bear, not what the treatment costs.

-76.98000,39.03400.name: FDA — intentional genomic alterations in animals
-76.98000,39.03400.desc: The US pathway for approving edited and engineered animals, which treats the introduced genetic change as an animal drug. That framing has been in place since 2009 and is why AquAdvantage salmon took twenty years: a drug approval requires evidence about the compound in every animal that receives it, which fits a veterinary medicine and does not fit a heritable trait. The agency has since created faster routes for low-risk alterations.

-90.73000,14.56000.name: ICTA — Instituto de Ciencia y Tecnología Agrícolas
-90.73000,14.56000.desc: Guatemala sits inside the centre of origin for maize, where wild relatives and thousands of local varieties still grow. Gene flow from an engineered crop into that diversity is a different question from gene flow in a field in Iowa, and this is the institute that holds the collections and would have to answer it.

-122.40300,37.65600.name: Twist Bioscience — DNA data storage
-122.40300,37.65600.desc: Writes digital data into synthesised DNA for archival storage, in a partnership including Microsoft and Illumina. Synthesis capacity built for data storage is the same capacity that makes genes, so a market with no biological purpose expands the infrastructure that biosecurity screening exists to watch.

-54.29600,-15.55600.name: Instituto Mato-Grossense do Algodão (IMAmt)
-54.29600,-15.55600.state: Primavera do Leste, Mato Grosso — experimental station
-54.29600,-15.55600.desc: A non-profit research institute created in 2007 by the members of the Mato Grosso cotton growers' association, and described by that association as its technological arm. It runs a cotton breeding programme aimed at yield, fibre quality and resistance to the diseases and nematodes of the region, a molecular biology laboratory at its experimental station, a network of trials across the state's cotton districts, and a plant protection department testing fungicides, herbicides and insecticides. Its published cultivar comparisons sit alongside the transgenic events sold by the multinationals. This is the third model in this facet: not an independent contractor selling studies, not a state institute, but a laboratory owned by the growers whose crop is being tested — which changes who the results are for.
